overview: The Sultanate of Rum was an Anatolian branch of the Seljuk dynasty, centered on cities including Konya. It developed from the late eleventh century and disappeared in the early fourteenth. The imported map is misleading: its 1279 to 1492 coverage omits most of the sultanate’s earlier history and keeps its label long after Seljuk rule had ended. Later outlines must not be read as a surviving Rum state.

items.text: The rulers of Rum shared ancestry with the Great Seljuks of Iran and Iraq, but the branches were separate and sometimes hostile. Their early history is poorly documented. Suleiman ibn Qutulmish is traditionally treated as the founder, while later sultans consolidated authority among other Turkish principalities and their Byzantine neighbors.

Konya was a royal burial place and important center, but the sultans did not stay in a single capital all year. They moved between Konya, Aksaray, Kayseri and the southern coast. Palaces and government activity existed in several cities. Following the court could therefore involve a journey, rather than a daily walk to one permanent office.

Caravanserais sheltered traders, their animals and their cargo along Anatolia’s routes. Their spacing reflected the distance a caravan could travel in a day, with about thirty kilometers given as a typical stage in the Turkish heritage description. Thick walls and protected courtyards combined practical accommodation with security. A tired animal needed a stopping place just as much as its driver.

At Kınık Höyük, bones from medieval features were dominated by sheep and goats, followed by cattle. Chickens, small numbers of geese and ducks, and hunted birds such as partridges also appeared. Researchers associate these remains with the twelfth- and thirteenth-century settlement. The finds reveal local food and animal use, without supplying a complete menu for every Anatolian household.

The same settlement produced horse, donkey, camel and dog remains, showing animals beyond those identified as food. Researchers also found turtles that seem to have died naturally around the site. A bone is not automatically a leftover meal. Careful examination of species, body parts and marks helps archaeologists decide what an animal was doing in a community.

The Huand Hatun complex at Kayseri included a bathhouse with separate sections for men and women, alongside a mosque, school and tomb. Its patron, Mahperi Khatun, was the mother of Sultan Kaykhusraw II. The mosque’s inscriptions date to 1237 or 1238; the other buildings are not individually dated. A royal woman’s foundation joined several kinds of urban activity in one place.

Kayseri’s Gevher Nesibe hospital and adjoining Gıyasiye school were built in 1205 or 1206 under Kaykhusraw I, following his sister Gevher Nesibe’s bequest, according to the official monument history. The paired buildings linked healthcare and learning. Much later repairs and restoration helped preserve them, so the museum visitors see today is not an untouched medieval hospital.

At Konya’s Karatay school, built in 1251 or 1252, rooms surrounded a covered courtyard with a pool beneath an opening in the dome. Students had small rooms, while winter classrooms provided more enclosed teaching spaces. Some student rooms were reconstructed in the 1970s. The layout makes a school’s practical needs visible: places to study, stay, and obtain light and air.

Rumi made Konya his home for most of his career and attracted students as well as patrons. His Persian poetry remained central to the Mevlevi tradition, developed into an organized order by his son Sultan Walad. Learning here included discussion, spiritual instruction and literary composition. Family connections helped carry a teacher’s work beyond his own lifetime.

sections.title: Making things and reading the evidence

items.text: At Kubadabad Palace beside Lake Beyşehir, star-shaped tiles fitted between cross-shaped pieces to form colorful wall panels. Their pictures include eagles, horses, lions, fantastic creatures and seated people. These were carefully made decorations for an elite residence. A palace wall could be crowded with animals even when none of them was actually in the room.

Kubadabad was a complex of buildings, work areas, water facilities and a bath, rather than one isolated hall. Stairway traces in the Small Palace indicate an upper floor. Historians date the royal complex to the 1230s using written testimony, the style of its tiles and tests on surviving wood. Different kinds of evidence fill gaps left by missing construction inscriptions.

Later workers reused parts of Kubadabad for workshops. A study of finds mainly from the late thirteenth century identified crucible fragments, steel blades and production waste as evidence of crucible steelmaking. The researchers place this activity under Ilkhanid or Turkish principality patronage. It belongs to the changing life of the palace site, rather than automatically to its first royal occupants.

“ضرب بمدينة قونية” means “struck in the city of Konya”. This Arabic phrase appears on a silver dirham of Qilij Arslan IV, dated 661 AH, or 1262 to 1263 CE. The Ashmolean catalogue transcribes it on the coin’s reverse. Along with a ruler’s titles and religious wording, the mint name helps turn a small piece of money into dated historical evidence.

ending.text: After defeat at Köse Dağ in 1243, the sultanate became subordinate to Mongol power. Its rulers gradually lost practical authority, and the precise final disappearance of the institution is poorly recorded. By the early fourteenth century it had ended, while rival principalities contested Anatolia. Konya, its communities and the Mevlevi tradition continued through these changes.
